title: AP Statistics
summary: Use the revised five-unit sequence to study design, probability, inference and regression.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the Fall 2026 five-unit revision, confirmed at https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-statistics/future-revisions. Historical nine-unit numbering is not used; removed slope-inference and goodness-of-fit topics are not presented as current requirements.

modules.title: Design a comparison before collecting data
modules.focus: Match an investigative question to a sampling or experimental design.
explanation: A useful statistical question identifies a population, variables and anticipated variation. A random sample supports generalisation to its sampling population. Random assignment creates treatment groups with a basis for a causal comparison; these two randomisation steps do different jobs.

Describe quantitative distributions using shape, centre, spread and unusual observations. Median and interquartile range resist extreme values better than mean and standard deviation. A summary must name the variable and its units, not merely list calculations.

workedExample.prompt: A school randomly assigns 60 volunteers to two study methods. What can the design support?
steps: Random assignment permits a causal comparison of the methods for participants, subject to execution and uncertainty.
Volunteering limits generalisation; assignment does not turn the volunteers into a random sample of all pupils.

misconception.claim: Random assignment automatically makes a sample representative.
misconception.correction: It balances treatment allocation in expectation, not selection into the study.

questions.prompt: For times 2,3,3,4,18 minutes, find the mean and median.
questions.hint: Sort the values and compare sensitivity to 18.

questions.prompt: A survey samples only library visitors to estimate all pupils’ reading habits. Identify a limitation.
questions.hint: Compare the sampling frame with the population.
questions.answer: Undercoverage: pupils who do not visit the library cannot be selected.
checkpoints: Explain how its habits may differ.

questions.hint: The frame is entrants at that gate during collection.
questions.prompt: A survey asks every tenth student entering one school gate. Identify a sampling-frame limitation.
questions.answer: Students using other gates or arriving outside the survey period may be excluded.
checkpoints: The frame is entrants at that gate during collection.
Not all pupils have a selection opportunity.
Generalisation to all pupils needs this limitation acknowledged.
hints: The frame is entrants at that gate during collection.
Not all pupils have a selection opportunity.

questions.hint: Treatment is applied to an individual plant.
questions.prompt: Twenty pairs of similar plants each receive treatments A and B, randomly allocated within pairs. Identify the experimental unit and reason for pairing.
questions.answer: Each plant is an experimental unit; pairing controls some initial plant variation.
checkpoints: Treatment is applied to an individual plant.
Similar plants are grouped before assignment.
Within-pair comparison reduces variation due to initial differences.
hints: Treatment is applied to an individual plant.
Similar plants are grouped before assignment.

notes.title: Reasoning through design a comparison before collecting data
paragraphs: Sampling and assignment answer different questions. Random sampling supports generalisation to the sampled population, whereas random assignment supports causal comparisons between experimental treatments. Blocking groups similar experimental units before randomising within groups to reduce irrelevant variation. A voluntary sample can still support a well-run randomised comparison among its participants, but it does not become representative merely through assignment. Confounding occurs when a competing explanation changes together with the explanatory variable. Replication reduces chance variation; it does not repair systematic selection bias or a consistently flawed measurement method.

workedExamples.prompt: An experiment compares two fertilisers on plots in sunny and shaded areas. Design a block randomisation.
steps: Separate plots into sunny and shaded blocks before assignment.
Randomly allocate each fertiliser within each block.
Compare treatment responses while accounting for block, using the same measurement procedure.
workedExamples.conclusion: Each fertiliser is represented in both light conditions, reducing confounding by sunlight.

flashcards.front: What does random assignment chiefly support?
flashcards.back: A causal comparison when the experiment is properly executed.

flashcards.front: What does random sampling chiefly support?
flashcards.back: Generalisation to the population represented by the sampling frame.

flashcards.front: Why block before randomising?
flashcards.back: To reduce variation from a known relevant characteristic.

flashcards.front: Does a large biased sample remove selection bias?

modules.title: Conditional probability and repeated trials
modules.focus: Choose the denominator from the condition.
explanation: Conditional probability P(A|B) measures the fraction of B outcomes that also satisfy A. Independence requires P(A|B)=P(A), when defined. Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so nonzero mutually exclusive events are not independent.

A binomial count requires a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes per trial and a constant success probability. Its mean is np and standard deviation √(np(1-p)). Check the modelling conditions before applying a formula.

workedExample.prompt: Among 40 club members, 16 cycle; 10 of the 16 cyclists wear helmets. Find P(helmet|cycles).
steps: The condition restricts the denominator to 16 cyclists.

misconception.correction: The two probabilities usually have different conditioning groups and denominators.

questions.prompt: Four independent trials have success probability 0.5. Find P(exactly 3 successes).
questions.hint: Count the four possible failure positions.

questions.prompt: A binomial count has n=100 and p=0.2. Find its mean and standard deviation.
checkpoints: Take the square root for standard deviation.

questions.prompt: Five independent trials each have success probability 0.2. Find the probability of no successes.
In 60 observations, 18 have A and 12 have B; 6 have both. Are A and B independent in this table?

notes.title: Reasoning through conditional probability and repeated trials
paragraphs: Conditional probability changes the reference group. P(A|B) uses only outcomes satisfying B in its denominator, while P(A and B) uses the whole sample space. Independence means conditioning on one event leaves the other’s probability unchanged; it is not the same as mutually exclusive events. A binomial model requires a fixed trial count, two outcomes, independent trials and constant success probability. Sampling without replacement can violate exact independence, although a small sampling fraction can justify an approximation. Expected count and standard deviation describe the distribution rather than the result of every repetition.

workedExamples.prompt: In 100 records, 40 show A, 25 show B and 10 show both. Test independence.
workedExamples.conclusion: The empirical table satisfies the independence equality.

flashcards.front: What is P(A|B)?
What equation characterises independence?
What is the binomial mean?
What is the binomial standard deviation?

modules.title: Estimating a population proportion
modules.focus: Interpret an interval as a method with repeated-sample coverage.
explanation: For a random sample, a large-sample confidence interval for one population proportion is p̂±z*√(p̂(1-p̂)/n). Check independence and sufficiently many observed successes and failures before using the normal approximation.

A confidence level describes how often the procedure captures the fixed population proportion across repeated samples. It is not the percentage of people inside the interval. Significance tests instead assess how unusual sample evidence would be under a stated null proportion.

workedExample.prompt: In a random sample of 400 pupils from a much larger population, 240 prefer a schedule. Use z*=1.96 for an approximate 95% interval.
steps: p̂=0.6 and standard error=√(0.6·0.4/400)≈0.02449; both observed counts exceed 10.

misconception.claim: A 95% interval contains 95% of individual responses.
misconception.correction: It estimates a population proportion, not a range of individual outcomes.

questions.prompt: If sample size quadruples with the same p̂ and confidence level, what happens to the margin of error?
questions.hint: Track the square root of n.

questions.prompt: A test has p-value 0.03 and α=0.05. State the decision, without claiming certainty.
questions.answer: Reject the null; the evidence is statistically significant at 0.05.
checkpoints: Rejection does not prove the alternative with certainty.

questions.prompt: With p̂=0.4, n=400 and z*=2, calculate the approximate confidence interval.
A two-sided test yields p=0.08 at α=0.05. State the decision and one conclusion it does not establish.
questions.answer: Fail to reject the null; this does not prove the null true.
checkpoints: Insufficient evidence against the null is not proof of equality.

notes.title: Reasoning through estimating a population proportion
paragraphs: A confidence interval estimates a fixed population proportion using a method with a stated long-run capture rate. After computing one interval, the frequentist confidence level is not a probability that the fixed parameter moves inside it. The normal approximation requires adequate success and failure counts and a design supporting independence. A test uses the null proportion in its standard error, whereas a common interval uses the sample proportion. A p-value measures compatibility with the null model under repeated sampling; it is neither the probability the null is true nor the effect’s practical importance.

workedExamples.prompt: A random sample has n=100 and 50 successes. Use z*=2 for an approximate interval, assuming independence.
steps: Both observed counts are 50, supporting the count condition.

flashcards.front: What does a 95% confidence procedure describe?
flashcards.back: About 95% capture over repeated samples under its assumptions.

flashcards.front: Which proportion enters a one-proportion null test standard error?
Does a small p-value measure effect size?
How does a fourfold sample increase affect the usual standard error?
flashcards.back: It halves it, holding the proportion fixed.

modules.title: Inference for a mean and paired change
modules.focus: Match the analysis to how observations were collected.
explanation: When a population standard deviation is unknown, inference for a mean uses the sample standard deviation and a t distribution. For one mean, the standard error is s/√n and degrees of freedom are n-1.

For before-and-after observations on the same people, analyse within-person differences rather than treating the groups as independent. Randomisation, independence between sampled units and a suitable shape or adequate sample size remain conditions, not optional decorations.

workedExample.prompt: A random sample of 25 independent changes has mean 4 and standard deviation 10. Using t*=2.064, calculate a confidence interval for the population mean change; assume the shape condition holds.

misconception.claim: Paired data should always be analysed as two independent samples.
misconception.correction: Pairing links the observations; analyse the differences to preserve that structure.

questions.prompt: For n=36, sample mean 18, s=6 and null mean 16, find the one-sample t statistic.
questions.hint: Divide the mean difference by s/√n.

questions.prompt: An interval for mean change is (-1.2,3.4). Does it exclude no average change?
questions.answer: No. Zero lies within the interval.
checkpoints: Use the interval for the population mean.
Do not conclude every participant had zero change.

questions.prompt: For n=25, mean difference 2, s=5 and null difference 0, find t and degrees of freedom.
An interval for after-minus-before is (−4,−1). Give the corresponding interval for before-minus-after and interpret the sign.
questions.answer: (1,4); before is estimated higher on average.
checkpoints: Reorder them from smaller to larger.
The entire reversed interval is positive.
hints: Reorder them from smaller to larger.

notes.title: Reasoning through inference for a mean and paired change
paragraphs: For paired data, define each difference in a consistent direction and analyse one sample of differences. The sample size is the number of complete pairs, not twice that number. A one-sample t statistic compares the sample mean with a null mean in units of estimated standard error s/√n. The t procedure accounts for estimating the population standard deviation, with n−1 degrees of freedom. Small-sample inference is sensitive to severe skewness or outliers. An interval containing zero permits no mean change as a plausible value, even when the observed mean difference is positive.

workedExamples.prompt: Sixteen independent paired differences have mean −3 and standard deviation 4. Use t*=2.131 for a confidence interval, assuming shape conditions.
workedExamples.conclusion: The interval is (−5.131,−0.869), entirely below zero in the defined difference direction.

flashcards.front: What is the observational unit in paired inference?
flashcards.back: One complete pair represented by its difference.

flashcards.front: What is the t standard error for a mean?
What are the degrees of freedom?
Why state the difference direction?
flashcards.back: Reversing it reverses every sign and the interpretation.

modules.title: Regression predictions and residuals
modules.focus: Measure an observation’s distance from its fitted prediction.
explanation: A least-squares line predicts a response from an explanatory variable by minimising squared vertical residuals. A residual equals observed response minus predicted response. A positive residual means the observation lies above the fitted line.

Correlation describes linear association and has no units. It does not establish causation. Prediction far beyond the observed input range is extrapolation and needs separate justification. A slope must be interpreted in response units per explanatory-variable unit.

workedExample.prompt: A model predicts reading time ŷ=12+3x minutes for x pages. A four-page reading takes 27 minutes. Find the residual.
steps: Residual=27-24=3 minutes, so the observed time is above the prediction.

misconception.claim: A strong correlation proves that changing x causes y to change.
misconception.correction: Confounding and study design still determine whether a causal conclusion is justified.

questions.prompt: For ŷ=8-0.5x, predict y at x=6.
A line is fitted using ages 12–18. Is predicting at age 60 interpolation?
checkpoints: The relationship may change outside that range.

questions.prompt: For ŷ=4+1.5x, find the prediction at x=6 and residual if y=11.
A regression slope is 2 dollars per item. If response values are converted to cents, what is the new slope and does correlation change?
questions.answer: Slope 200 cents per item; correlation is unchanged.
checkpoints: The slope scales by the same positive factor.
A positive unit change leaves correlation unchanged.
hints: The slope scales by the same positive factor.

notes.title: Reasoning through regression predictions and residuals
paragraphs: A least-squares line predicts the response from the explanatory variable within the context of the observed data. A residual is observed minus predicted response and retains the response’s units. A positive residual means the observation lies above the fitted line. Residual patterns can reveal curvature or changing spread that a single correlation coefficient hides. The slope describes predicted change per input unit, not automatically a causal effect. Extrapolation beyond the observed range adds model uncertainty. Correlation is unitless and linear; a strong nonlinear relationship can have a weak linear correlation.

workedExamples.prompt: A line predicts ŷ=50−2x. At x=8 the observed response is 30. Find and interpret the residual.
steps: The observation is four response units below the line.

flashcards.front: What is a residual?
What does a positive residual mean?
flashcards.back: The point is above the fitted line.

flashcards.front: Does regression alone establish causation?
What can a curved residual pattern suggest?
flashcards.back: A straight-line model misses systematic structure.
